# STATUS "Open questions" Must Be Written Inline, Not Pointed At

The `/closeout` skill changed between runs to require that a repo's `STATUS.md` `## Open questions` section state each question in full — the question plus enough context to answer it — rather than referring the reader to another file. On 2026-10-04 the `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` STATUS violated this by pointing at `PLAN.md`, and was rewritten. The reason is mechanical: `where-was-i.py --decisions` extracts the section's text, so a pointer like "See PLAN.md" yields no decisions and the questions never reach the next morning's `/startup` list.

## Key Points

- **The consumer cannot dereference.** A script that reads one section and prints its contents has no mechanism for following a cross-file reference, so a pointer is equivalent to an empty section.
- **The failure is an omission, not a corruption.** The extractor returns nothing rather than returning something wrong, so nothing in the morning list signals that items were dropped.
- **Context travels with the question.** The requirement is not just the question text but enough surrounding detail to answer it, because the reader arrives at it with no memory of the session that raised it.
- **The cost lands on exactly the blocked items.** On 2026-10-04 the dropped questions were the ones the deliverable was gated on: DEXA data placement, athlete data in `Ath_Medicine` / `Catapult_API` / `S2_Evaluation`, and the ITS routing-sheet position.
- **Skills change under you.** The closeout run had to notice that its own instructions had moved since the last pass, which is itself an argument for re-reading the skill rather than replaying the remembered procedure.

## Details

This is the reverse of the usual documentation instinct. Good practice normally says not to duplicate a rule in two places, because two copies drift — the lesson recorded for paired policy and athlete-facing documents. That rule holds when both copies are read by humans who can notice and reconcile a difference. It inverts when one copy is read by a program with a fixed extraction contract: there the pointer form is strictly worse, because dereferencing is not a capability the consumer has, and the resulting silence is indistinguishable from "no open questions." Drift is detectable on inspection; omission is not.

The practical rule that falls out is to write the machine-readable field for its actual consumer and accept the duplication, while keeping the authoritative discussion wherever it belongs. In this case `PLAN.md` can still hold the full reasoning; `STATUS.md ## Open questions` must independently carry the question and enough context that someone reading only the morning decision list can act. The same logic explains why the 2026-10-04 closeout also pushed `global-memory` and `~/.claude` the same evening rather than waiting for the nightly job — the next consumer was a different machine starting work before the scheduled window, so the handoff had to be placed where that consumer would actually look.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/ncaa-best-practices-doc-draft-verification]] — The repo whose STATUS was rewritten, and the open questions that would otherwise have been dropped.
- [[concepts/same-day-context-repo-push]] — The sibling closeout decision from the same session, also driven by where the next consumer will look.
- [[connections/write-the-decision-where-each-consumer-will-look]] — Placement follows how the next reader arrives at the question; deferrals need the record more than completed work does.
- [[connections/machine-readable-fields-cannot-hold-pointers]] — The general rule: single-source-of-truth and write-it-inline are split by whether the field's consumer can dereference.
- [[concepts/paired-document-single-source-of-truth]] — The opposite case, where duplication is the defect because both readers are human.
- [[concepts/machine-split-workday-closeout]] — The closeout ritual this requirement lives inside.

# Filename Dates Lie: Establishing Document Currency Before Reuse

Before drafting the Applied Performance Digest on 2026-10-04, a parallel search established which of several candidate source documents were actually current. Two findings inverted the apparent chronology. Iowa's Sports Performance Assessment Manual exists as near-identical copies labelled 2017, a 2021 draft, and a May 2024 PDF — but the "May 2024" file is textually identical to the 2017-11-06 copy: same 27 pages, same 5,085 words, same 2017 creation metadata. And Baylor's November 2025 `.docx`, the only copy newer than its own May 2024 PDF, proved 97.5% identical to it at word level, differing only in the table of contents, one table position, and one phrase.

## Key Points

- **A filename or distribution date records when a copy was circulated, not when its content was written.** The Iowa "May 2024" PDF is 2017 text by metadata and by word-for-word comparison.
- **Three independent signals agreed:** page count, word count, and PDF creation metadata all placed the content in 2017, which is what made the conclusion safe to act on.
- **Near-identity is as important a finding as staleness.** Baylor's Nov 2025 and May 2024 copies being 97.5% identical means the February 2026 gap analysis built against the older copy still applies in full — no re-analysis needed.
- **The currency check determined the base document.** The Nov 2025 `.docx` was adopted as the content base because it is newest, with the PDF kept only for page references.
- **The search also corrected a naming assumption:** no Iowa file is literally a "playbook"; the source is the Sports Performance Assessment Manual, so the remembered name would not have found it.

## Details

The cost of skipping a currency check is asymmetric and silent. Treating the Iowa "May 2024" PDF as 2024 material would have imported seven-year-old protocol conventions as current peer practice, with the file's own name as the apparent warrant. Conversely, treating the Baylor November 2025 copy as substantially new would have triggered an unnecessary re-run of the February 2026 gap analysis — work that the 97.5% diff proved pointless. Both errors are invisible from the file listing, which is the only view most source-selection decisions get. What made them visible was cheap, mechanical comparison: diff the two copies, count words, read the PDF's creation metadata.

This generalizes a pattern recorded elsewhere in the knowledge base about reading metadata rather than running or trusting an artifact — the same move that diagnosed a stale install-time environment capture by inspecting its recorded version instead of executing it. Here the artifact is prose rather than a virtualenv, but the discipline is identical: the object's self-description is evidence, and it frequently contradicts the label someone attached to the container. The practical procedure is short enough to make routine before any document reuse — enumerate every copy, compare them pairwise, read creation metadata, and only then decide which is the base and what the others are good for. A related loose end from the same session shows the limit of the method: "AP Assessment Manual V12" is named in Flint provenance notes but was not found on disk or on Drive, so a document can be cited by a name that resolves to nothing at all.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/peer-document-reuse-boundaries]] — What each source was then permitted to contribute once its currency was known.
- [[connections/install-time-environment-capture-rots-silently]] — The same diagnostic move: read the artifact's recorded metadata rather than trusting its surface or running it.
- [[connections/documented-paths-decay-verify-at-use]] — The time axis of decay applied to paths; this is the same decay applied to content.
- [[concepts/rounded-counts-in-context-documents]] — Recording a quantity at an abstraction level that matches its stability, or stamping it with a verification date.
- [[connections/a-stale-pointer-resolves-cleanly-to-the-wrong-answer]] — A filename date resolves successfully while returning the wrong answer about the content behind it.

# Independent Verification of a Delegated Subagent Run

When the Applied Performance Digest's chapter-01 build was delegated to a Fable subagent on 2026-10-04, the subagent's completion report was not accepted as evidence. Two disciplines were applied: the subagent pasted raw verification output rather than summarizing it, and the parent session then re-ran the checks itself. Five checks were verified independently — files exist, chapter 01 is 2,858 words against an 800-word minimum, zero em dashes across all Digest files plus STATUS/README/CLAUDE, the branch matches origin, and no credentials were copied from the Clemson source.

## Key Points

- **A completion report is a claim, not an artifact.** The subagent reporting "done, verified" is a summary produced by the same process whose output is in question.
- **Raw output beats a summary.** Requiring the subagent to paste command output preserves the evidence in a form the parent can read, rather than compressing it into a judgment.
- **Re-running is cheap for exactly these checks.** File existence, a word count, an em-dash grep, a branch comparison, and a credential scan are all seconds-long and mechanical — there is no cost argument for trusting the report instead.
- **The checks are objective and pre-stated.** Each has a single right answer knowable without judgment, which is what makes independent re-execution meaningful rather than a second opinion.
- **Two of the five checks guard against inherited defects,** not against the subagent's own work: zero em dashes enforces house style, and the credential scan ensures the Clemson source's plain-text passwords and staff names were not reproduced.

## Details

Delegation moves work out of the parent's context, which is the point — but it also moves the evidence out, and the report that comes back is a lossy, self-interested summary. The pattern recorded here closes that gap in two stages. Asking for raw output addresses fidelity: the parent sees what the commands actually printed rather than the subagent's reading of them, which is the same reason an agent-produced summary is disqualified as verification of the document it summarizes. Re-running the checks addresses independence: even faithful raw output came from the delegated process, so a parent that re-executes is producing a second derivation that can be diffed against the first. The two together convert "it says it worked" into "I observed it working."

What makes this tractable is the shape of the checks. Each one is a single-answer, no-judgment question — does this path exist, is this number above that floor, does this grep return zero hits, does this ref match. That is the same property that makes a numbered harness-agnostic check list portable across models and sessions, and it is why verification of a delegated run should be designed at delegation time rather than invented afterward: the parent decides what the objective success criteria are, states them in the prompt, and then has something re-runnable when the report arrives. Checks requiring judgment — whether the prose is any good, whether the outline is complete — cannot be verified this way, which is precisely why chapter 01 still carries 27–28 unresolved `[CONFIRM]` tags and an outstanding `articulation` pass. Objective verification establishes that the delegated run did what it was told; it does not establish that the result is shippable.

# Three Postures for Reusing Peer and External Documents

The 2026-10-04 Applied Performance Digest build assigned each of its five source documents an explicit reuse posture rather than treating them as one undifferentiated pile of input. Three distinct postures emerged: Baylor's own newest copy became the *content base*; Iowa's Sports Performance Assessment Manual and Clemson's material were used for *format, structure, and ideas only*, with Clemson's plain-text passwords and staff names deliberately not reproduced; and the NCAA best-practices guide with its forms A–E was *linked rather than rewritten*, with that repo left unedited.

## Key Points

- **Content base vs. format source is the primary split.** Only the organization's own document may supply substantive content; peer manuals supply shape.
- **Peer documents carry contaminants that must be stripped by rule, not by noticing.** Clemson's material contained plain-text passwords and named staff — exactly the material that gets copied accidentally when a document is used as a template.
- **Linking beats absorbing for a live sibling deliverable.** The NCAA guide and forms A–E are maintained in their own repo under their own review process, so the Digest references them instead of copying their text.
- **"Leave the source repo unedited" is part of the posture.** Consuming a deliverable does not license modifying it, which keeps the two artifacts' review histories separate.
- **The postures were decided before drafting,** which is what let the credential-scan check be stated as an objective pass/fail condition on the delegated run's output.

## Details

Assigning a posture per source converts a judgment that would otherwise be made repeatedly and inconsistently during drafting into a single decision made once. Without it, each paragraph of each peer document invites the same question — is this something we adopt, adapt, or merely admire — and the answer drifts toward adoption because adopting is less work. The format-only rule for Iowa and Clemson is especially load-bearing given what the currency investigation found: Iowa's apparently-2024 manual is 2017 text, so adopting its content would have imported stale conventions, while adopting its *structure* costs nothing because document organization does not expire the way protocol specifics do.

The credential question generalizes beyond this one document. A peer institution's internal manual is an operational artifact, and operational artifacts contain operational secrets and personnel details that are harmless in their home context and inappropriate anywhere else. Treating "no credentials or staff names copied" as a stated, checkable condition on the output — rather than as something the drafter should be careful about — is what makes the rule survive delegation to a subagent that has no particular reason to notice a password embedded mid-document. The third posture, linking rather than rewriting, answers a different risk: the NCAA guide was itself under active review the same evening, with a five-item fix list pending, so any text copied into the Digest would have been a snapshot of a document known to be changing. Pointing at it keeps a single source of truth and avoids the paired-document drift that the same day's audit found between a guide's access matrix and its athlete-facing appendix.

# Inspect the Built Artifact Rather Than Re-Running the Build

During the 2026-10-04 read-only verification of Baylor's Performance Technology Best Practices guide, the twelve PDF deliverables were examined with PyMuPDF rather than by re-running `scripts/build_guide.py`. The reason was that the build drives Microsoft Word through COM, so re-running it would have produced Word automation side effects during a pass that was explicitly meant to be non-mutating. The inspection confirmed what the audit needed — the guide at 9 pages and each of Appendices A–E at 2 pages, all rendering correctly — without touching the generator.

## Key Points

- **"Read-only" has to include the build step.** A verification pass that regenerates its subject is not read-only, regardless of whether any source file is edited.
- **The generator can have side effects outside the repo.** A COM-driven Word build manipulates an application and its state, so its blast radius is not bounded by `git status`.
- **The artifact is the thing under audit.** Page counts, rendered text, and layout are properties of the PDF, and the PDF is what will be sent — reading it directly answers the actual question.
- **Programmatic PDF reading is sufficient for structural checks.** PyMuPDF gave page counts and extractable text, which covered checks on build artifacts, pending tags, terminology, and styling.
- **Fixes still route through the generator.** The five prose corrections were recorded as edits at `scripts/build_guide.py` lines 98, 108, 160, 218, and 358 — inspect the output, edit the source.

## Details

The distinction worth preserving is between *verifying* and *reproducing*. Reproducing a build demonstrates that the generator still runs and produces the same output; verifying an artifact asks whether the artifact in hand is correct. Those are different questions with different costs, and for a document deliverable the second is both the cheaper one and the one that matters, because the PDF already exists and is what will reach the audience. Re-running the build to check the PDF conflates them and imports the generator's side effects — here, driving a GUI application through COM — into what should be a pure observation.

The complementary half of the pattern is that *corrections* go to the generator, not the artifact. The audit's five prose fixes were specified as line edits in `build_guide.py` rather than as changes to the PDFs, because a hand-edited PDF is destroyed by the next build. This is the same reasoning behind fixing the generator rather than the artifacts when mangled outputs recur, and it means the read/write asymmetry is deliberate: read downstream where the truth is, write upstream where it persists. One residual hazard the session noted is that the generator's own correctness is not established by this method — if `build_guide.py` had a layout bug the inspection would catch its *effect* in the PDF, but a build that silently failed to pick up a source change would be invisible until the next full run.

# Native Windows Python Cannot Open a Git Bash /tmp Path

A document-extraction script written during the 2026-10-04 Digest build failed because it wrote output to a Git Bash `/tmp` path. Git Bash presents a POSIX-style filesystem rooted in its MSYS installation, but a native Windows Python interpreter does not participate in that translation: it resolves `/tmp/...` against the current drive root, producing a path like `C:\tmp\...` that does not exist. The fix recorded in the repo's STATUS Gotchas section was to anchor output relative to the script's own directory rather than to an absolute POSIX path.

## Key Points

- **The POSIX root is a Git Bash illusion, not a system fact.** MSYS translates paths for processes it launches through its own layer; a native Windows interpreter sees the literal string.
- **The failure is a confusing one rather than an obvious one.** `/tmp` resolves to a syntactically valid Windows path under the current drive, so the error is "no such directory" rather than "malformed path."
- **The durable fix is relative anchoring.** Deriving the output location from the script's own file location removes the dependency on any shell's notion of a root.
- **This is the same hazard as writing handoffs to `/tmp`** on a Unix host for a different reason — the path resolves somewhere, just not somewhere useful or persistent.
- **Cross-shell scripts should avoid absolute paths in either dialect.** A path that works in Git Bash may fail in PowerShell and vice versa; a script-relative path works in both.

## Details

This belongs to a well-populated family of Windows findings in which a tool's environment assumptions do not survive being handed to a different executor. Claude Code's hooks run through bash even when the interactive shell is PowerShell, so PowerShell-syntax hook commands fail; `setx` writes the registry while running processes keep their launch-time environment; Task Scheduler spawns with a minimal PATH that bare executable names cannot resolve. The common structure is that one layer's conventions — shell syntax, environment snapshot, PATH, filesystem root — are assumed to be universal and are not. Here the assumed-universal convention is the POSIX filesystem root, and the executor that does not share it is `python.exe`.

The practical rule generalizes past this one case. Any absolute path written into a script encodes an assumption about which layer will interpret it, and on a mixed Windows/Git Bash machine that assumption is frequently wrong and always invisible until something runs. Anchoring to the script's own directory removes the assumption entirely rather than replacing it with a better one — the same move as making a synced config reference `$HOME`-relative rather than picking whichever absolute path is correct on the current host. The failure is also cheap to miss during development: a developer who happens to run the script from a shell whose translation layer *does* apply will see it work, and the breakage appears only when the invocation path changes.

# Connection: Scope Definition Lives in Prior Handoffs, Not in the Prompt

## The Connection

On 2026-10-04 the Applied Performance Digest's `/goal` prompt was written, and then a nine-day-old handoff note — `RunningTheRoom/docs/handoffs/2026-09-25-answers-self-audit-myelin-cleanup.md` — was read and found to define the Digest as three parts: a handbook, an operations manual, and NCAA technology items. The prompt named four sources and omitted the third part entirely. `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc` had to be added as a fifth source, without which the outline would have missed roughly a third of the deliverable. The same day's closeout established the mirror-image requirement from the writing side: a repo's `STATUS.md` open questions must be stated inline, because a pointer to another file never reaches the next session's decision list.

## Key Insight

Scope omissions are silent in a way that scope errors are not. A prompt that asks for the wrong thing produces output someone recognizes as wrong; a prompt that asks for two thirds of the thing produces output that is correct, complete-looking, and internally consistent across everything it covers. Nothing in the artifact points at the missing third. The only place the full definition existed was a handoff note written nine days earlier by a session that had since ended, which means the goal prompt's correctness depended on a document outside the prompt's own repo.

That asymmetry sets the operational rule in both directions. When *starting* work, search prior handoffs for a scope definition before writing the goal prompt — the prompt is a reconstruction from memory and memory is exactly what handoffs exist to replace. When *finishing* work, write the scope and the open questions into the place the next consumer will actually read, in a form that consumer can read: inline prose in `STATUS.md ## Open questions` for a script that cannot dereference a pointer, in the project directory rather than `/tmp` for a note that must survive a reboot, and in the repo rather than only in a transcript.

## Evidence

- **The omission was a third of the deliverable.** The handoff defined handbook + ops manual + NCAA tech items; the prompt covered the first two. Catching it required reading the handoff, not reviewing the prompt.
- **The reading happened in parallel with source-currency work,** not as a dedicated scope check — so the catch was partly incidental, which is the argument for making it a step.
- **The closeout found the symmetric defect in the repo being worked on.** `NCAA_BestPractices_Doc`'s STATUS pointed at `PLAN.md`, making its open questions invisible to `where-was-i.py --decisions` and absent from the next `/startup` list — exactly the failure that nine days later produces a prompt missing a third of its scope.
- **Prior instances of lost placement decisions:** a handoff written to `/tmp/` was wiped on reboot and invisible to a home-directory search, and staged-but-uncommitted fixes were lost across a session break. Each is the same loss at a different layer.
- **The self-reinforcing loop is visible in one day.** The Digest was rescued by a good handoff; the NCAA repo's bad handoff field was fixed so the next session's prompt would not need rescuing.

# Connection: Machine-Readable Fields Cannot Hold Pointers

## The Connection

Two findings from 2026-10-04 give opposite advice about writing the same information twice. The verification of the Performance Technology Best Practices guide found that duplicating one access rule in a staff-facing matrix and an athlete-facing disclosure let the two copies drift, and prescribed a single source of truth. The closeout of the same repo found that `STATUS.md ## Open questions` must *not* point at `PLAN.md` but restate each question inline, duplicating content that already exists elsewhere. Both are correct, and the variable that selects between them is whether the field's consumer can dereference a pointer.

## Key Insight

A human reader can follow "See PLAN.md," and can also notice when two prose copies of a rule disagree. A script reading one section cannot do either: `where-was-i.py --decisions` extracts the section's text and prints it, so a pointer yields nothing and the duplication it would have avoided is never at risk. The consumer's capability, not editorial taste, decides the form.

The deeper asymmetry is in the failure modes. Drift — the cost of duplication — is *detectable*: both copies exist, a reader or a diff can compare them, and the February 2026 gap analysis survived precisely because a 97.5% word-level comparison could be run. Omission — the cost of a pointer a consumer cannot follow — is *undetectable*: the morning `/startup` list simply has fewer items, and nothing distinguishes "no open questions" from "three open questions in an unreachable file." Given a choice between a detectable failure and an undetectable one, duplicate. That is the same preference ordering behind generating derivable state rather than maintaining it, where mod load lists, prose job counts, and untracked skill copies all failed by omission; generation is the best option because it removes both failures, and inline duplication is the fallback when generation is impractical.

## Evidence

- **Pointer form, machine consumer, silent loss.** NCAA STATUS said "See PLAN.md"; `where-was-i.py --decisions` returned nothing; the DEXA-storage, `Ath_Medicine`/`Catapult_API`/`S2_Evaluation`, and ITS routing-sheet questions would never have reached the next morning's list. The closeout skill was changed to require the question plus enough context to answer it.
- **Duplicated form, human consumers, detectable drift.** Guide §4.3 grants Athletic/Applied Performance flags only on raw wellness data while Appendix A says Athletic Performance sees wellness check-ins; both read correctly in isolation and the conflict is visible only on comparison — and *was* found by comparison.
- **The derived-instrument variant widens rather than narrows.** Appendix A's general research checkbox appears to satisfy Guide §4.5's IRB-plus-study-specific-consent rule, and Appendix B's N/A column bypasses rows the guide calls mandatory; the fix in each case was an explicit, auditable trace rather than deletion of the second copy.
- **The generation option, where available, dominates both.** A load list derived from the `mods/` folder exposed Windows loading 6 of 8; a count re-derived at audit time cannot be stale. Where the artifact can be generated, neither drift nor omission is possible.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data without saving changes to it.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

profile.description: Loads a saved browser profile without saving changes to it.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, `developer`, or `gov`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns results in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; `firecrawl_gov_search` is the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
